Name: shallow_alignment_depth
Title: Alignment Is Shallow: Safety Lives in the First Few Generated Tokens
Short Hypothesis: Safety fine-tuning primarily alters the conditional distribution of the first few response tokens (the refusal 'preamble') rather than deep capability suppression; therefore safety is brittle to any perturbation that gets past the opening tokens, and deepening alignment beyond token-1 measurably improves robustness.
Related Work: Qi et al. (2024, 'Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep'); Zou et al. (2023) prefix attacks; Andriushchenko et al. (2024) refusal via prefilling. Qi et al. introduce the shallow-safety observation and a data-augmentation fix. We distinguish by mechanistically characterizing *which* components implement the shallow signal via per-token attribution, and by testing an interpretability-guided training objective that redistributes safety signal across response depth, comparing mechanistic depth metrics before and after.
Abstract: Prefilling attacks—forcing a model to begin its answer with an affirmative token—reliably bypass safety, suggesting alignment is concentrated in the first few output tokens. We hypothesize that safety fine-tuning predominantly reshapes early-token conditionals and that this shallowness is both measurable at the mechanism level and correctable. We quantify safety 'depth' by measuring KL divergence between aligned and base models across response-token positions and by per-token attribution of the refusal direction, expecting a sharp concentration at positions 1-5. We then test whether a training objective that supervises safety at deeper token positions (via harmful-continuation data where refusal must emerge mid-response) redistributes the mechanism, measured by a flatter depth profile and increased robustness to prefilling and mid-sequence injection. We evaluate attack success under prefill, suffix, and mid-response injection attacks; capability retention; and over-refusal, comparing standard safety tuning, Qi et al.'s augmentation, and our depth-aware objective. We predict base alignment is sharply shallow, that robustness correlates with our mechanistic depth metric, and that deepening the mechanism improves resistance to prefill/injection with modest capability cost. The contribution is a mechanistic definition and metric of alignment depth that predicts robustness, turning a behavioral observation into a diagnostic and training target.
Experiments: 1) Compute per-token-position KL(aligned || base) on harmful prompts; plot depth profile. 2) Per-position refusal-direction projection to localize where safety signal lives. 3) Attacks: prefill ('Sure, here is'), GCG suffix, mid-response injection; measure ASR. 4) Train depth-aware objective: augment with harmful dialogues requiring mid-response refusal; retrain safety. 5) Re-measure depth profile and ASR; report correlation between depth metric and robustness. 6) Capability: MMLU, GSM8K; over-refusal: XSTest. Models: Llama-3-8B base+instruct, Qwen2.5-7B.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Depth metric may not cleanly predict robustness across attack types. Deepening safety could increase over-refusal or harm fluency. Requires retraining, compute-intensive. Mid-response refusal data is hard to construct realistically. Findings may vary with alignment recipe (RLHF vs DPO).
